line: Did you know, Brixton's Barrier Block was shaped as a wall against a motorway that was never built?
fact: Southwyck House on Coldharbour Lane curves round in a 176-flat horseshoe to shield its estate from Ringway 1, an inner London motorway later dropped.

line: Did you know, many Windrush arrivals settled in Brixton because the nearest job centre to their shelter was there?
fact: In 1948, 236 Windrush passengers with nowhere to go slept in a shelter under Clapham Common. The nearest labour exchange was on Coldharbour Lane.

line: Did you know, the butterfly called the Camberwell beauty is named after two found on Coldharbour Lane in 1748?
fact: The rare butterfly is named after 2 found on Coldharbour Lane in 1748. They had probably stowed away on timber ships from Scandinavia.

line: Did you know, the future Prime Minister John Major spent part of his childhood in a flat on Coldharbour Lane?
fact: As a boy, the future Prime Minister John Major lived in a flat on Coldharbour Lane, Brixton, from 1955 to 1959.

line: Did you know, the Brixton nightclub the Fridge opened above a frozen food shop?
fact: In 1982 the club the Fridge moved in above Iceland on Brixton Road, decorated with battered ice boxes and fake dead cats hung from the ceiling.

line: Did you know, Laurel and Hardy once played a Brixton music hall that's now housing?
fact: The Empress opened in 1898 and later hosted Marie Lloyd, Vera Lynn and Laurel and Hardy. It became a cinema, then bingo, and was knocked down in 1992.

line: Did you know, the band Basement Jaxx found their sound in the back room of a Brixton Hill pub?
fact: From 1994 the band Basement Jaxx ran a club night at the back of the George IV pub. They said its chaos shaped their music. It became a Tesco in 2013.

line: Did you know, a windmill off Brixton Hill was still making flour for West End hotels in the 1930s?
fact: Ashby's Mill was built in 1816. It lost its sails in 1862 but kept grinding by steam, then gas, sending flour to West End hotels until 1934.

line: Did you know, Brixton prison was one of the first to put prisoners on a treadmill?
fact: In 1821 Brixton prison, then the Surrey House of Correction, was one of the first to bring in a treadmill. Prisoners trod it to grind corn.

line: Did you know, Brixton prison became a women's jail because Tasmania stopped taking England's women convicts?
fact: In 1852 Van Diemen's Land, now Tasmania, became the last colony to refuse women convicts from England, so Brixton prison was turned over to women.

line: Did you know, Brixton prison's execution shed was never used and became a gym for the staff?
fact: Brixton prison built an execution shed in 1902. Nobody was ever hanged in it, and it was turned into a gym for the staff.

line: Did you know, an 1806 law is why so much of Brixton Road sits back behind gardens?
fact: An 1806 Act banned building within 150 feet of the road across Rush Common. So Brixton Road's houses were set back, and Windrush Square stayed open.
source: Wikipedia: Brixton Library; Brixton; Windrush Square

line: Did you know, Windrush Square began as a garden bought by Henry Tate's wife when the council wouldn't pay?
fact: In 1901 Lambeth thought £3,000 too much for the land by Brixton's library. In 1904 Amy Tate paid £3,250 for it and gave it to the council as a garden.

line: Did you know, the bronze commuters on Brixton station's platforms were cast from real locals?
fact: For the 1986 statues the artist chose 3 locals, 2 of them staff at the leisure centre opposite, and made their moulds in a disused ticket office.

line: Did you know, St Matthew's church in Brixton was one of the churches built to celebrate victory at Waterloo?
fact: St Matthew's, finished in 1824 on land taken from Rush Common, was one of the Waterloo churches, built to celebrate Britain's win at Waterloo.
source: Wikipedia: St Matthew's Church, Brixton; Brixton

line: Did you know, Brixton Academy was bought for £1 in 1983?
fact: The 1929 Astoria cinema on Stockwell Road had failed as a disco and then a rock venue when a buyer paid £1 for it in 1983 and opened Brixton Academy.

line: Did you know, the band Leftfield once played Brixton Academy so loud that the ceiling started to fall?
fact: In 1996 the dance band Leftfield hit 137 decibels at Brixton Academy. The bass brought dust and plaster down from the ceiling, and the rig was banned.

line: Did you know, the MP who opened Brockwell Park died on the steps of its hall that day?
fact: Brockwell Park opened to the public in 1892, led by the local MP. During the ceremony he had a heart attack and died on the steps of Brockwell Hall.

line: Did you know, about 150,000 people filled Brockwell Park for a Rock Against Racism concert in 1978?
fact: In 1978 about 150,000 came to a Rock Against Racism carnival in Brockwell Park, headlined by the singer Elvis Costello. Some watched from trees.

line: Did you know, Brockwell Lido was saved by two former council workers after Lambeth shut it?
fact: Lambeth closed the 1937 lido in 1990 to save money. Two former council workers then won the contract to run it and reopened it in 1994.

line: Did you know, Brixton Road was once called the Washway, after the stream that ran beside it?
fact: Until about 1850 Brixton Road was the Washway, after the River Effra flowing beside it. The river was covered over in 1847 and runs in a sewer below.

line: Did you know, Brixton's buried River Effra may take its name from a lost local manor called Heathrow?
fact: The Effra had no known name before the late 1700s. Lambeth's archivist thinks it came from Effra Farm, once the manor of Heathrow, by Effra Road.

line: Did you know, two Black Panthers squatted on Railton Road in 1972 and fought off eviction?
fact: In 1972 two women from the British Black Panthers took over a flat above a Railton Road launderette, then opened number 121, squatted until 1999.

line: Did you know, a Railton Road dress shop hid an unlicensed bar for Caribbean gay men in the 1970s?
fact: Under her dress shop at 103 Railton Road, the artist Pearl Alcock ran an unlicensed bar for Caribbean gay men, until police closed it in 1979.

line: Did you know, a cycle track in a Herne Hill park held Olympic races in 1948?
fact: Herne Hill Velodrome, a shallow concrete bowl built in 1891 in a park off Burbage Road, hosted the track cycling at the 1948 Olympics.

line: Did you know, Brixton had its own money, with David Bowie on the 10 pound note?
fact: From 2009 Brixton shops took the Brixton pound. Later notes showed David Bowie on the B£10 and the wartime secret agent Violette Szabo on the B£20.

line: Did you know, the tiles in Brixton tube station's seat alcoves are a pun on its name?
fact: Every Victoria line station got its own tile design in the seat alcoves. Brixton's, from 1971, shows a ton of bricks.

line: Did you know, police stopped almost 1,000 people in Brixton in 5 days just before the 1981 riot?
fact: In April 1981 plain-clothes police were sent into Brixton. In 5 days they stopped almost 1,000 people, mostly young black men. Rioting followed.

line: Did you know, Brixton Village market was nearly replaced by a 10-storey tower in 2008?
fact: In 2008 new owners planned to replace the 1937 Granville Arcade with a 10-storey tower. Traders and locals fought it off, and it was listed in 2010.

line: Did you know, Jamaican arrivals in 1948 were housed in an air-raid shelter under Clapham South station?
fact: In 1948 a ship brought 492 people from Jamaica to fill London's jobs. With nowhere else to house them, many slept in the shelter under Clapham South.

line: Did you know, Benjamin Franklin calmed a pond on Clapham Common with a teaspoon of oil?
fact: In the early 1770s the American statesman Benjamin Franklin poured a teaspoon of oil on a Clapham Common pond and calmed the water for yards around.

line: Did you know, Samuel Pepys spent his last years in Clapham, in the house of his old servant?
fact: The diarist Samuel Pepys spent his last 2 years in Clapham, in the house of his old servant and friend William Hewer. He died there in 1703.

line: Did you know, Captain Cook's widow lived on Clapham High Street for many years?
fact: After the explorer Captain James Cook was killed, his widow Elizabeth lived for many years in a house at 136 Clapham High Street.

line: Did you know, a first-century Roman stone was placed by the old library in Clapham Old Town?
fact: Clapham High Street follows a Roman road. A 1st-century stone recording it was dug up nearby in 1912 and placed by the old Clapham Library.

line: Did you know, the founder of the Clapham Sect was the great-grandfather of the man behind the Venn diagram?
fact: Henry Venn, the Holy Trinity curate who started the anti-slavery Clapham Sect, was great-grandfather to John Venn, who came up with the Venn diagram.

line: Did you know, a slave trader worshipped in the same Clapham church as the anti-slavery campaigners?
fact: Wilberforce's anti-slavery circle prayed at Holy Trinity on Clapham Common. So did George Hibbert, a merchant and slave trader who opposed him.

line: Did you know, two mounds on Clapham Common are left over from a Second World War gun site?
fact: In the Second World War Clapham Common had a heavy anti-aircraft gun site. Two mounds on the Battersea Rise side are left from its storage bunkers.

line: Did you know, Clapham Junction isn't in Clapham, and was named that to sound posher?
fact: Clapham Junction is in Battersea and was first called Battersea Junction. The railways took Clapham's name to attract a richer class of passenger.
source: Wikipedia: Clapham Junction railway station; Clapham

line: Did you know, Bertrand Russell first gave his talk Why I Am Not a Christian at Battersea Town Hall?
fact: The philosopher Bertrand Russell first gave Why I Am Not a Christian as a talk in 1927, at Battersea Town Hall, which is now Battersea Arts Centre.

line: Did you know, Battersea chose a Black mayor in 1913?
fact: In 1913 Battersea made John Archer, a Black councillor for Latchmere, its mayor. He was elected at the town hall on Lavender Hill.

line: Did you know, Lavender Hill is named after the lavender once grown on its slopes for sale?
fact: Lavender Hill is named after lavender grown on it for sale. By 1774 the name was known: a man offered a reward for a pony lost from a field there.

line: Did you know, laundresses once bleached linen on the grass at the east end of Lavender Hill?
fact: In the early 1800s a row of cottages at the east end of Lavender Hill housed laundresses, who bleached and dried linen on the grass behind them.

line: Did you know, the Bank of England helped plan the gold robbery in the film The Lavender Hill Mob?
fact: For the 1951 comedy The Lavender Hill Mob, about a Lavender Hill clerk who robs his own bank of gold, the Bank of England set up a committee to help.

line: Did you know, Northcote Road runs over a buried stream?
fact: Northcote Road sits low between Clapham and Wandsworth commons because it lies over the Falconbrook, a stream now hidden in a culvert.

line: Did you know, the Who built their own studio in a Battersea church hall to make Quadrophenia?
fact: In 1973 the band the Who turned a church hall on Thessaly Road into a studio to record their album Quadrophenia. It later became a doctors' surgery.

line: Did you know, Battersea Dogs Home began in a woman's scullery in Holloway?
fact: Mary Tealby started a home for lost and starving dogs in her scullery in Holloway in 1860. The Times mocked her. It moved to Battersea in 1871.

line: Did you know, Battersea Dogs Home looked after 145,000 dogs during the Second World War?
fact: In the Second World War Battersea's manager urged owners not to put pets down for fear of food shortages. It fed and cared for over 145,000 dogs.

line: Did you know, Benedict Arnold, the American who changed sides, is buried in a Battersea church?
fact: Benedict Arnold fought for George Washington, then changed sides and became a British officer. He lies in the crypt of St Mary's, Battersea.

line: Did you know, Ronnie Biggs of the Great Train Robbery escaped from Wandsworth prison?
fact: In 1965 Ronnie Biggs escaped from Wandsworth prison, partway through 30 years for the Great Train Robbery. He fled to Brazil, on the run until 2001.

line: Did you know, Wandsworth prison kept its gallows working until 1993, decades after the last hanging?
fact: The last hanging at Wandsworth was in 1961, yet its gallows were tested every 6 months until 1993. The condemned cells became an officers' tea room.

line: Did you know, 34,000 people from occupied Europe were questioned for spies in a Wandsworth orphanage?
fact: In the Second World War, 34,000 people from occupied Europe were questioned for spies in this old Wandsworth orphanage. 50 were confirmed as agents.

line: Did you know, the girls in Wandsworth's Crimean War orphanage had to pump water up its towers?
fact: Crimean War orphan girls at the Royal Victoria Patriotic School pumped water up to its towers, did the washing and were washed outside in cold water.

line: Did you know, Chelsea Bridge was first called Victoria Bridge, until it seemed it might fall down?
fact: Chelsea Bridge opened in 1858 as Victoria Bridge. Doubts over its safety led the government to rename it, so a collapse wouldn't be tied to the Queen.

line: Did you know, the Celtic Battersea Shield was dredged from the Thames while Chelsea Bridge was built?
fact: Digging the riverbed for Chelsea Bridge's piers in the 1850s turned up Roman and Celtic weapons, skeletons and the bronze and enamel Battersea Shield.

line: Did you know, the Duke of Wellington fought a duel as prime minister on what's now Battersea Park?
fact: In 1829 the prime minister, the Duke of Wellington, fought a duel with an earl on Battersea fields. The duke aimed wide; the earl fired into the air.

line: Did you know, a brewer kept brewing weekly at the closed Ram Brewery to keep its oldest-brewery claim?
fact: After the Ram Brewery closed in 2006, a former Young's brewer kept a tiny brewery there going weekly, to keep its claim as Britain's oldest brewery.

line: Did you know, Clapham was once so ordinary that its bus passenger came to stand for everyone?
fact: In the early 1900s Clapham was such a plain commuter suburb that the man on the Clapham omnibus came to mean any ordinary person.

line: Did you know, Stockwell's first tube carriages were winched up a steep tunnel to their depot on a wire rope?
fact: Stockwell's first tube carriages reached their depot up a tunnel so steep, 1 in 3.5, that they were winched up on a wire rope until 1907.

line: Did you know, 2 wartime tunnels under Stockwell station could shelter about 4,000 people?
fact: Two tunnels under Stockwell station, finished in 1942, could shelter about 4,000 people. One entrance, brightly painted, is now a local landmark.

line: Did you know, Stockwell's huge bus garage was built of concrete because steel was short after the war?
fact: Steel was short when Stockwell bus garage was built for 200 buses in 1952, so its roof was made of concrete: 10 shallow arches with no pillars.

line: Did you know, before he became a painter, Vincent van Gogh lodged on Hackford Road while selling art?
fact: In 1873, at 20, Vincent van Gogh came to London to work for an art dealer. He rented a room at 87 Hackford Road from a mother and daughter.

line: Did you know, Kennington had a royal palace until Henry VIII took it apart to build Whitehall?
fact: The Black Prince built a royal palace near Kennington Cross after 1337. In 1531 Henry VIII had most of it taken down and reused at Whitehall Palace.

line: Did you know, St Mark's Church opposite Oval station was built on the site of Kennington Common's gallows?
fact: Kennington Common was south London's hanging ground until its last hanging in 1799. In 1824 St Mark's church went up where the gallows had stood.

line: Did you know, the Chartists' great 1848 rally on Kennington Common was organised by a Black Londoner?
fact: In 1848 the Chartists, a working-class movement for the vote, held their biggest rally on Kennington Common. Its organiser, William Cuffay, was Black.

line: Did you know, people killed in a 1940 air raid still lie under Kennington Park?
fact: In October 1940 a bomb hit a trench shelter in Kennington Park, killing about 100. The wet walls kept caving in, so up to 54 more were left buried.

line: Did you know, Bob Marley often visited a Rastafarian temple in a squatted street by Kennington Park?
fact: From 1969 squatters took over St Agnes Place, built for Buckingham Palace servants, and set up a Rastafarian temple. Bob Marley often went in 1977.

line: Did you know, Kennington's Cinema Museum is in the old workhouse young Charlie Chaplin was sent to?
fact: At 7, Charlie Chaplin was sent to the Lambeth Workhouse when his family ran out of money. Its master's house and chapel now hold the Cinema Museum.

line: Did you know, the Oval cricket ground was a cabbage patch until 1845?
fact: In 1844 the Oval was a Duchy of Cornwall cabbage patch. In spring 1845, 10,000 turfs from Tooting Common were laid, and cricket began that May.

line: Did you know, in the Second World War the Oval was made a camp for enemy parachutists?
fact: In the Second World War the Oval cricket ground became a prisoner-of-war camp for enemy parachutists. None ever landed, so it was never used.

line: Did you know, Cleaver Square was built by a pub landlord on a pasture called White Bear Field?
fact: Cleaver Square was a pasture called White Bear Field. In 1780 Mary Cleaver leased it to a Kennington pub landlord, who built the square.

line: Did you know, the Imperial War Museum's home was the Bethlem asylum, and its dome housed the chapel?
fact: The Imperial War Museum moved in 1936 into what had been Bethlem, London's old asylum. Its 2 long wings were knocked down to make a park.

line: Did you know, the Russian word for a railway station comes from Vauxhall's pleasure gardens?
fact: Russians named their pleasure gardens after Vauxhall's. So many stood near railway stations that the Russian word for Vauxhall came to mean station.

line: Did you know, Vauxhall's old pleasure gardens kept unlit dark walks for lovers?
fact: Vauxhall's pleasure gardens, open until 1859, were lit by thousands of lamps. Their unlit dark walks were known as the place for secret romance.

line: Did you know, police who raided the Royal Vauxhall Tavern in 1987 wore rubber gloves?
fact: Police raided the gay pub the Royal Vauxhall Tavern in 1987 in rubber gloves, against AIDS, a minister said. The drag act Lily Savage was arrested.

line: Did you know, Vauxhall Bridge has 8 huge bronze statues that can't be seen from the bridge?
fact: In 1907, 8 bronze statues of about 2 tons each were fixed above Vauxhall Bridge's piers. They can only be seen from the banks or from boats.

line: Did you know, in 1844 a clown sailed from Vauxhall Bridge to Westminster in a washtub pulled by geese?
fact: In September 1844 crowds packed Vauxhall Bridge to watch a clown from Astley's circus sail to Westminster Bridge in a washtub, towed by geese.

line: Did you know, the MI6 building at Vauxhall has 2 moats?
fact: The MI6 building at Vauxhall, opened in 1994, has triple-glazed windows, 2 moats, and much of the building below street level.

line: Did you know, MI6's secret headquarters from 1964 was an office block on Westminster Bridge Road?
fact: From 1964 MI6 was based at Century House on Westminster Bridge Road. Its address was officially secret, yet a paper said every taxi driver knew it.

line: Did you know, Lambeth Bridge is red, the colour of the benches in the House of Lords?
fact: The Lords sit at the end of Parliament nearest Lambeth Bridge. Westminster Bridge, by the Commons end, is green like the Commons benches.

line: Did you know, Lambeth Palace had its own prison at the top of a tower?
fact: The archbishops of Canterbury kept a prison room at the top of the stairs in the palace's Lollards' Tower, built in the 1430s.

line: Did you know, the Garden Museum began when a visitor found Lambeth's old church boarded up for demolition?
fact: In 1976 Rosemary Nicholson came to see the tomb of 2 royal gardeners and found St Mary's shut. She saved it and opened a museum of garden history.

line: Did you know, Royal Doulton's Lambeth pottery was closed in 1956 by clean air rules?
fact: From 1815 Doulton made stoneware jars and drainpipes in Lambeth. The pottery closed in 1956, when clean air rules stopped salt glazing in cities.

line: Did you know, Doulton's Lambeth pottery was unusual in letting its artists sign their work?
fact: From 1871 Doulton's Lambeth pottery hired artists from the local art school, Hannah Barlow among them. Unusually, they signed their own pieces.

line: Did you know, St Thomas' Hospital moved to Lambeth because a railway was built over its old site?
fact: St Thomas' Hospital was in Southwark from the Middle Ages until 1862, when a railway took its land. It reopened opposite Parliament in 1871.

line: Did you know, Florence Nightingale kept a pet owl that travelled in her pocket?
fact: Florence Nightingale rescued an owl in Athens, raised it by hand and called it Athena. It went everywhere in her pocket, and is now in her museum.

line: Did you know, coffins leaving Waterloo for the cemetery travelled first, second or third class?
fact: From 1854 a private line ran the dead from Waterloo to a Surrey cemetery. Coffins had class tickets too, and first class cost £1.

line: Did you know, golfers dressed as mourners to ride the cheap funeral train out of Waterloo?
fact: Fares on the coffin train never changed for 85 years. Golfers posed as mourners to reach a golf course on the cemetery company's spare land.

line: Did you know, parts of Waterloo station were once nicknamed Cyprus and Khartoum?
fact: Waterloo grew in bolt-on sections, each with its own entrance and booking office. One, from 1878, was called Cyprus, and one from 1885 Khartoum.

line: Did you know, a Paris councillor asked Tony Blair to rename Waterloo station?
fact: When Eurostar came to Waterloo, a Paris councillor asked Tony Blair to rename it. A station named after Napoleon's defeat upset the French, he said.

line: Did you know, the Kinks' song Waterloo Sunset was first called Liverpool Sunset?
fact: The Kinks' 1967 song Waterloo Sunset began as Liverpool Sunset. The band changed it as there were already too many songs about Liverpool.

line: Did you know, a star actor at the Old Vic told his audience they were ignorant brutes?
fact: In 1824 the actor Edmund Kean played six Shakespeare plays in six nights there, then said he had never acted to such "ignorant, unmitigated brutes".

line: Did you know, an 18-year-old black American actor played at the Old Vic in 1825?
fact: In 1825 Ira Aldridge, a black American actor of 18, played the Old Vic in a play against slavery. He became one of the great stars of his day.

line: Did you know, Morley College began in the Old Vic's dressing rooms?
fact: Emma Cons turned the rowdy Old Vic into a coffee hall with penny lectures. They led to Morley College, taught in its dressing rooms until the 1920s.

line: Did you know, a Lambeth music hall's crowd reached their seats through a tunnel with an aquarium?
fact: In 1859 the railway into Waterloo cut the Canterbury music hall off from its entrance. Crowds got in by a tunnel under the tracks with an aquarium.

line: Did you know, a Lambeth music hall had a glass roof that slid back to let the cigar smoke out?
fact: The Canterbury, rebuilt for 1,500 in 1856, was a pub music hall where waiters served at tables. Its glazed roof could open to clear the smoke.

line: Did you know, the size of circus rings around the world was set by a Lambeth showman?
fact: Philip Astley opened his ring on Westminster Bridge Road in 1773. He settled on 42 feet across, about 13m, still the circus standard.

line: Did you know, the black circus rider Pablo Fanque first performed in London at a Lambeth circus?
fact: Pablo Fanque, a black horse rider and circus owner, made his London debut in 1847 at Astley's, a circus on Westminster Bridge Road.

line: Did you know, the stone lion by Westminster Bridge was painted red for 15 years?
fact: The 1837 lion came off a brewery knocked down for the Festival Hall. Painted red as British Rail's symbol, it was stripped when moved in 1966.

line: Did you know, the South Bank Lion had its maker's initials and a date hidden under a paw?
fact: When the lion came down from the old Lion Brewery, the sculptor's initials and the date 24 May 1837 were found under one of its paws.

line: Did you know, the Royal Festival Hall stands where a woman ran a factory making artificial stone for royal palaces?
fact: Where the Royal Festival Hall stands, Eleanor Coade made a weatherproof artificial stone from 1769 to 1821. Kings used it in their palaces.

line: Did you know, the Royal Festival Hall once used hidden microphones and speakers to fix its dry sound?
fact: Microphones in the ceiling fed lost sound back through speakers. As the system aged it made odd noises during concerts, and was switched off in 1998.

line: Did you know, a student climbed the Skylon at midnight and tied a scarf near the top?
fact: In 1951, days before the King's visit, a student climbed the 90m Skylon at midnight and tied a scarf near the top. A policeman went up for it.

line: Did you know, bits of the Festival of Britain's Skylon tower were made into paper knives?
fact: Churchill had the Skylon taken down in 1952, seeing it as a symbol of Labour's Britain. It was sold for scrap, and some became paper knives.

line: Did you know, the Festival of Britain had a cinema showing 3D films and the new invention of television?
fact: The Festival of Britain's Telecinema showed 3D films and television to about 460,000 people in 1951. Afterwards it became BFI Southbank.
source: Wikipedia: Festival of Britain; BFI Southbank

line: Did you know, London's council hung slogans on County Hall for MPs to read across the river?
fact: In the 1980s the Labour-run Greater London Council, at war with Thatcher's government, hung opposition slogans on County Hall, facing Parliament.

line: Did you know, builders of the Shell Centre dug into an abandoned air-powered railway?
fact: Builders of the Shell Centre found an abandoned air-powered railway, dug from 1865 to run under the Thames to Charing Cross until the money ran out.

line: Did you know, the Shell Centre was built with a rifle range and a swimming pool in its basement?
fact: Finished in 1962, the oil firm's tower gave staff a full-size pool, a gym, a rifle range, a snooker room and their own supermarket underground.

line: Did you know, a light sculpture on the Hayward Gallery's roof changed with the wind for 36 years?
fact: From 1972 to 2008 a neon sculpture on the Hayward Gallery's lift tower changed with the wind. Taken down to be fitted with LEDs, it never went back.

line: Did you know, the London Eye began as an entry in a newspaper contest that nobody won?
fact: In 1993 two architects, a married couple, entered a design for a millennium landmark. The judges chose no winner, so they remortgaged their home.

line: Did you know, the London Eye was built lying flat on the river and then hauled upright?
fact: The London Eye came up the Thames on barges and was assembled lying flat on platforms in the river. Then it was raised at 2 degrees an hour.

line: Did you know, Waterloo was called Lambeth Marsh until the station came?
fact: Waterloo was the village of Lambeth Marsh, on a raised road across the marshes. The name Waterloo only took over after the station opened in 1848.

line: Did you know, Lambeth North station has had four names?
fact: It opened in 1906 as Kennington Road, became Westminster Bridge Road that July, Lambeth (North) in 1917 and Lambeth North in 1928.

line: Did you know, the National Theatre's foundation stone was laid 25 years before it opened?
fact: The stone went down in 1951, but 10 years on the government said the nation couldn't afford a national theatre. It opened in 1976.
source: Wikipedia: Royal National Theatre; The Old Vic

line: Did you know, the graffiti tunnel under Waterloo station began with a street art festival run by Banksy?
fact: Leake Street, a 300m road tunnel under the tracks, was first painted at the Cans Festival that Banksy organised in May 2008.
